excerpts.text: We write $\|\cdot\|$ for the Euclidean norm and $I_{d}$ for the $d\times d$ identity matrix. For symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$ , the notation $A\preceq B$ means that $B-A$ is positive semidefinite.

Let $O(n):=\{O\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:O^{\top}O=I_{n}\}$ denote the real orthogonal group, equipped with Haar probability measure. It has two components, $\{\det O=+1\}$ , $\{\det O=-1\}$ , and each have Haar probability $1/2$ . For $b\in\{-1,+1\}$ , we write $\mu_{n,b}$ for Haar probability measure conditioned on $\det O=b$ .

We restrict the target class to centered Gaussians. This restriction removes the hardness of locating the target and isolates the difficulty of sampling with an unknown covariance. For an integer $d\geq 1$ and a parameter $\kappa\geq 1$ , without loss of generality, we normalize the spectral bounds to $1$ and $\kappa$ by rescaling and consider the precision class
$\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}:=\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:A=A^{\top},\quad I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}\right\}.$

An input $A\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}$ specifies the quadratic potential $f_{A}(x):=\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax$ and the target distribution $\pi_{A}:=N(0,A^{-1})$ . At a point $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the exact first-order oracle returns
$\operatorname{FO}_{A}(x):=\bigl(f_{A}(x),\nabla f_{A}(x)\bigr)=\left(\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax,Ax\right).$ (1)

On this class, exact first-order access is equivalent to exact matrix–vector access. Indeed, a first-order response contains $Ax$ , while a matrix–vector response determines both the gradient $Ax$ and the function value $\frac{1}{2}\langle x,Ax\rangle$ . Thus the exact value-and-gradient, gradient-only, and matrix–vector query complexities coincide.

A randomized algorithm chooses its queries and stopping decisions as Borel functions of its internal randomness and previous oracle responses, where the randomness is independent of the input. Its output may be any $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ -valued Borel function of the same information. The algorithm has fixed query budget $T$ if it makes at most $T$ queries for every admissible input and every realization of its internal randomness.
For probability measures $P$ and $Q$ on a common measurable space, their total variation distance is
$\operatorname{TV}(P,Q):=\sup_{B}|P(B)-Q(B)|=\frac{1}{2}\int|p-q|\,d\lambda,$

where the supremum ranges over measurable sets, and $p$ and $q$ are the densities of $P$ and $Q$ with respect to any common dominating measure $\lambda$ . In particular, $|\mathbb{E}_{P}h-\mathbb{E}_{Q}h|\leq\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)$ for every measurable function $h$ taking values in $[0,1]$ .
For a fixed input $A$ , let $\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}$ denote the law of the algorithm’s output, with all internal randomness included. For $0<\varepsilon<1$ , define

$Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon):=\inf\left\{T\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}:\begin{array}[]{l}\exists\,\mathrm{Alg}\text{ with fixed query budget }T\\[2.0pt] \text{such that }\displaystyle\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}}\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}},\pi_{A}\bigr)\leq\varepsilon\end{array}\right\}.$ (2)

The accuracy requirement is uniform over inputs and concerns the output law after averaging over the algorithm’s seed. Throughout the paper, query budgets are deterministic caps on the number of queries in each run, rather than bounds on the expected number of queries.

Fix $\kappa\geq 4$ . Let $3\leq n\leq d$ be the block dimension and $k:=\lfloor d/n\rfloor$ the number of blocks. In the proof of the main theorem, we choose $n=2T+1$ , where $T$ is the algorithm’s query budget. This choice applies when $T\geq 1$ and $2T+1\leq d$ . The remaining cases are treated separately. For $O\in O(n)$ , define
$A_{O}:=\frac{\kappa+1}{2}I_{n}-\frac{\kappa-1}{4}(O+O^{\top}).$ (4)
For $\bm{O}=(O_{1},\ldots,O_{k})\in O(n)^{k}$ , set
$A_{\bm{O}}:=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(A_{O_{1}},\ldots,A_{O_{k}},I_{d-kn}\bigr).$ (5)

For each $b\in\{-1,+1\}$ , draw $O_{1},\ldots,O_{k}$ independently from $\mu_{n,b}$ , and let $\mathcal{D}_{b}$ denote the law of $A_{\bm{O}}$ . Thus the orthogonal matrices share the same determinant sign.
Writing $P_{b}:=\mathbb{E}_{O\sim\mu_{n,b}}[N(0,A_{O}^{-1})]$ for the single-block target mixture, the averaged target under $\mathcal{D}_{b}$ is
$\bar{\pi}_{b}:=\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\mathcal{D}_{b}}[\pi_{A}]=P_{b}^{\otimes k}\otimes N(0,I_{d-kn}).$ (6)
When $kn=d$ , the identity block and the final Gaussian factor are omitted.

We first separate the single-block mixtures using a bounded radial test, and then amplify this separation across independent blocks. The single-block argument combines a cancellation identity for Gaussian normalization factors with two spherical Poisson identities. Throughout this section, $n\geq 3$ , $\kappa\geq 4$ , and $O$ is Haar distributed on the full orthogonal group $O(n)$ . Write $U:=O_{11}$ , let $p_{O}$ be the density of $N(0,A_{O}^{-1})$ , and let $p_{b}$ be the density of $P_{b}$ , for $b\in\{-1,+1\}$ .
For $n\geq 3$ and $\kappa\geq 4$ ,
$\operatorname{TV}(P_{+1},P_{-1})\geq\frac{\left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}\right)^{n}}{2+\frac{4n\sqrt{\kappa}}{(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)^{2}}}\geq\frac{1}{2}e^{-5n/\sqrt{\kappa}}.$ (19)

Under each prior, the $k$ blocks of a target sample are independent and have the same single-block mixture law. We convert the preceding separation into an upper bound on Hellinger affinity, which multiplies across independent blocks.
Let $a$ denote the single-block Hellinger affinity:
Cauchy–Schwarz and $\int p_{+1}=\int p_{-1}=1$ give $0\leq a\leq 1$ and

$\displaystyle\operatorname{TV}(P_{+1},P_{-1})$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}|\sqrt{p_{+1}}-\sqrt{p_{-1}}|(\sqrt{p_{+1}}+\sqrt{p_{-1}})$ $\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}(\sqrt{p_{+1}}-\sqrt{p_{-1}})^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}(\sqrt{p_{+1}}+\sqrt{p_{-1}})^{2}\right)^{1/2}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{(2-2a)(2+2a)}=\sqrt{1-a^{2}}.$
Proposition B.7 therefore implies
$a\leq\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}e^{-10n/\sqrt{\kappa}}}\leq\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{8}e^{-10n/\sqrt{\kappa}}\right\},$ (25)
where the last inequality follows from $\log(1-t)\leq-t$ for $0\leq t<1$ .
Let $\bar{p}_{b}$ be the density of $\bar{\pi}_{b}$ . When $kn<d$ , write $\varphi_{d-kn}$ for the standard Gaussian density on $\mathbb{R}^{d-kn}$ . By Eq. (6),
$\bar{p}_{b}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k},z)=\prod_{j=1}^{k}p_{b}(x_{j})\,\varphi_{d-kn}(z).$
Tonelli’s theorem and $\int\varphi_{d-kn}=1$ give

$\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\sqrt{\bar{p}_{+1}(x)\bar{p}_{-1}(x)}\,dx$ $\displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{k}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\sqrt{p_{+1}(x_{j})p_{-1}(x_{j})}\,dx_{j}\right)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d-kn}}\varphi_{d-kn}(z)\,dz$ $\displaystyle=a^{k}.$
When $kn=d$ , the same identity holds with the Gaussian factor omitted. Finally, $\min\{u,v\}\leq\sqrt{uv}$ for $u,v\geq 0$ implies

$\displaystyle\operatorname{TV}(\bar{\pi}_{+1},\bar{\pi}_{-1})$ $\displaystyle=1-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\min\{\bar{p}_{+1}(x),\bar{p}_{-1}(x)\}\,dx$ $\displaystyle\geq 1-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\sqrt{\bar{p}_{+1}(x)\bar{p}_{-1}(x)}\,dx$ $\displaystyle=1-a^{k}$ $\displaystyle\geq 1-\exp\left\{-\frac{k}{8}e^{-10n/\sqrt{\kappa}}\right\},$
where the last step uses Eq. (25). ∎
